cues.text: The start of a new academic year is a challenge for booksellers. Lee Rogers talks to one major book store manager.
cues.speaker: Announcer

cues.text: Jenny Farrow, you're the manager of Dalton Books - and you sell an awful lot of books to students, don't you?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: Yes! We do.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: How do you manage to make sure that you're going to have the books students need when all the new courses begin?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: Basically, we make preparations long before they arrive. Like all other major book retailers, we have a database of information, and using that, we contact course convenors in May and ask them to send us their booklists.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: How many books are we talking about?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: For one course?
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: Yes, as an example.
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: An average course requires about 30 books. We ask lecturers to indicate whether a book is what we call 'essential' reading ... you know, the students simply have to get it ... or whether it's what they would term ' recommended' reading or whether it's just a supplementary text that they tend to refer to as 'background' reading.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: What about predicted buyers?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: It's not a perfect system unfortunately. If a lecturer tells us that he expects us to sell 100 copies of a book, we know that we could actually sell anything from 50 to 150. That's why in practice, when it comes to ordering, it's a lot safer to ao by the previous year's sales figures - if that's possible of course … if we've sold the book before. We also build other factors into the equation including the type of course that the books are for, the students' year group and a measure of our own judgement.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: And these criteria make a fairly accurate guide?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: As accurate as we can be, yes.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: What about the publishers? Do they take an active role in promoting new books?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: Certainly. The academic and professional publishing market is worth about £700 million a year, so publishers go to some lengths to make sure their books are known. The standard procedure they use is to mail out catalogues to lecturers or colleges and universities, that's been the main form of promotion for years. Now, of course, they can also post details of new or revised works on websites. Some even go so far as writing individual letters to the appropriate lecturers in order to let them know what's coming up.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: The lecturers then contact you if they're interested ...
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: That's right. The publishers send us - the book sellers - ' inspection copies'. Lecturers can then get a free copy and decide whether it's going to be suitable for their course
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: And how does it work with the students? What are they looking for and who helps them most?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: I think lecturers are best placed to understand the students' needs. Often the critical issue is what represents value for money for students. This is more important than price per se.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: Do students actually buy books before they start the course?
cues.speaker: Lee

cues.text: Apparently a large proportion of students wait to see what they need. Students have a firm idea of what constitutes a good book so they tend to give themselves time to look at all the options before making a choice. They tend to go for books that are clear and easy to use. Often the texts that their lecturers recommend turn out to be too academic and remain here on our shelves.
cues.speaker: Jenny

cues.text: Well that was Jenny ...
cues.speaker: Lee
